t: Good Indices in a Digit String
o:
Index `i` is good when the decimal string of `i` appears in `s` ending exactly at position `i`. Since the representation of `i` has a fixed length `len(str(i))`, there is exactly one candidate substring: `s[i-L+1 .. i]`. So each index is checked in O(L) time — no searching needed.

Example 1: at i=11 the representation '11' has length 2, and s[10..11]='11' matches. At i=12, s[11..12]='12' matches. Other indices fail. Constraints (n up to 1e5, representations up to 6 digits) mean the direct check is about 6e5 character comparisons — trivially fast.
k: The substring ending at i that could equal str(i) is uniquely determined by its length.

a.i: For each index, slice out the last `len(str(i))` characters and compare with `str(i)`. Correctness is immediate: any matching substring must have exactly that length and must end at `i`.
s: For each i from 0 to n-1, let t = str(i), L = len(t).
If i - L + 1 >= 0 and s[i-L+1..i] == t, record i.
a.t: O(n · d) where d ≤ 6 is the maximum digit count — each index does one short comparison

a.n: Approach 2: Try every start position (brute force)
a.i: For each index i, try every substring ending at i and compare with str(i). This is strictly worse but demonstrates the naive reading of the statement and is still fast enough for n = 1e5 only if we break early by length; practically it is O(n^2) and included mainly as a baseline.
s: For each i, for each start j from i down to 0, compare s[j..i] with str(i).
Stop scanning starts once the substring is longer than str(i).
a.t: O(n · d) in practice since the inner loop runs at most d times — effectively identical to Approach 1

w: Always prefer Approach 1 — the length of str(i) pins down the only candidate window. Pitfall: forgetting the leading-zero rule is irrelevant here (indices never have leading zeros), but watch the boundary when the representation is longer than i+1 characters (early indices with multi-digit... actually only i=0 has this risk with '0'). Follow-up: count good indices without building substrings, using rolling hashes.
